name: Fluridil

lead: Fluridil is a topical antiandrogen sold in Europe as Eucapil for pattern hair loss. People look to it for slower thinning and fuller hair without lowering hormones throughout the body.

Its developers describe it as suppressing the androgen receptor locally in the scalp, so follicles are less affected by androgens, while being highly hydrophobic, easily broken down by hydrolysis and not absorbed into the body. The published evidence is a 2002 randomised trial in 43 men, which reported a higher percentage of hairs in the growth (anagen) phase than placebo and no changes in sexual function or lab values.

paras: It is a lotion applied to the scalp as part of a regular hair-loss routine, used by people who want a non-systemic option. Hair-cycle changes build over months.

The 2002 study found no irritation or sensitisation in patch tests and normal sexual function and blood values, but it was small and short, and long-term data are not available. It is not an approved drug in the US.

angle.text: Fluridil, sold in Europe as Eucapil, is a topical antiandrogen that blocks androgen receptors in the scalp, so follicles shrink less and thinning slows. People use it as a non-systemic option for fuller hair. Its clinical data come from a 2002 trial in 43 men.

lead: Fluridil (marketed in Europe under the name Eucapil) is a topical antiandrogen developed for androgenetic alopecia. Its authors describe it as a novel agent that suppresses the human androgen receptor locally in the scalp, is highly hydrophobic and breaks down by hydrolysis, and is not absorbed systemically.[1]

The published clinical evidence is a single early study: a 2002 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 43 men with androgenetic alopecia, reported alongside a patch-test safety study in 20 men.[1] The trial reported an increase in the proportion of hairs in the anagen (growth) phase, and no changes in sexual function, libido, blood counts or blood chemistry.[1] No larger or independent trials appear in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Sold in Europe; not an approved drug in the US (per the sources reviewed, no approval is described)

paras: According to the researchers who developed it, fluridil is a rationally designed topical antiandrogen that suppresses the human androgen receptor. It is highly hydrophobic and hydrolytically degradable, and the authors describe it as systemically non-resorbable. In animal studies they reported high local and general tolerance.[1] Because it acts on the receptor rather than on 5-alpha-reductase, it is mechanistically distinct from finasteride and dutasteride.

In the 2002 trial, 43 men with androgenetic alopecia (Norwood grade II to Va) used 2 percent fluridil or placebo. Baseline anagen and telogen counts were equal in all groups. After three months the average anagen percentage was unchanged in placebo subjects but rose from 76 percent to 85 percent in fluridil subjects and to 87 percent at nine months. Former placebo subjects who then received fluridil rose from 76 to 85 percent after six months.[1] The abstract reports phototrichogram-based hair-cycle outcomes; the sources reviewed do not describe hair counts, density or cosmetic ratings from independent trials.

In the patch-test arm, 20 men received occlusive forearm patches with 2, 4 and 6 percent fluridil, isopropanol and vaseline over 21 days; neither fluridil nor isopropanol showed sensitisation or irritation potential, unlike vaseline.[1] In the main trial, sexual function, libido, haematology and blood chemistry were reported as normal, and blood analysis for fluridil itself was included.[1] The trial was small and short, and long-term safety data are not available in the sources reviewed.

Fluridil appears in T Nation hair-loss threads as an option alongside RU58841 and other topical antiandrogens, with users describing it as lesser known; one poster says that for someone on testosterone, its 'cost to benefit ratio nose-dives' relative to other choices, and another says they 'haven't learned much about this one yet'.[2][3]

One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical study (43 men with androgenetic alopecia) and a 20-man patch-test study were published in 2002, reporting increased anagen percentage and no sexual, haematological or biochemical changes.[1] No other human trials were found in the sources reviewed.

lore.intro: Fluridil is mentioned occasionally on T Nation as one of several lesser-known topical antiandrogens, usually next to RU58841, and is described as obscure.[2][3]

claims.claim: Fluridil is a topical antiandrogen option for hair loss that avoids systemic effects

timeline.event: First clinical experience with 2 percent fluridil in men with androgenetic alopecia published in Dermatologic Surgery.[1]
